title: Twenty tests, one false alarm
objectives: See how running many tests produces false discoveries.

screens.title: Twenty signals, one hit
screens.prose: A colleague builds 20 trading signals from pure noise, on purpose. None can predict anything. She tests each one at the 5% level, and one passes.

state.caption: Dashed marks: the 5% cut-off, $|z| = 1.96$. Signal 18 has $|z| = 2.39$, so $p = 0.017$.

screens.question: Signal 18 passed. What should you conclude?

options.text: Signal 18 has a real edge, at 95% confidence
options.why: You read one pass as a discovery. Every signal here is noise, and a 5% test passes noise one time in 20.

options.text: Nothing: one pass in 20 noise tests is the usual result
The test is faulty, since noise should never pass
options.why: A 5% test is built to pass noise 5% of the time. One pass in 20 is exactly that rate.

options.text: There is a 1.7% chance that signal 18 is noise
options.why: You turned $p$ around. $p = 0.017$ is the chance noise gives a $|z|$ this big, not the chance the signal is noise.

hints.text: How often does a 5% test pass when there is nothing to find?
All 20 bars are noise. Only one crosses the cut-off.
Each noise test passes with chance 0.05, so 20 of them expect $20 \times 0.05 = 1$ pass.

feedback.correct: One pass in 20 is what pure noise usually gives.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Remember that all 20 signals are noise by construction.

byKey.edge: You read one pass as a discovery. Every signal here is noise, and a 5% test passes noise one time in 20.

explain.text: All 20 signals are noise, yet one crossed the line. A 5% test passes noise one time in 20, so 20 tests expect one pass. The pass tells us how many tries were made, not that signal 18 works.

screens.title: The family's error rate
screens.prose: The chance of at least one false alarm across a family of tests is the **family-wise error rate**, FWER. Each test alone has $\alpha = 0.05$. The curve is the FWER for $N$ independent tests on noise.
screens.question: Compute the FWER for 20 independent tests at $\alpha = 0.05$. Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Find the chance that all 20 tests stay quiet first.
One noise test stays quiet with chance 0.95.
Independent tests multiply: $0.95^{20} = 0.3585$. The FWER is $1 - 0.3585$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance that no test passes, then take the complement.

byKey.added: You added 20 chances of 0.05. Overlapping chances do not add: two tests can both pass.
byKey.none: That is the chance all 20 stay quiet. The FWER is the chance at least one does not.
byKey.alpha: That is one test's chance, not the family's.

explain.text: No false alarm needs all 20 tests quiet: $0.95^{20} = 0.3585$. The FWER is the complement, $1 - 0.3585 = 0.6415$. That matches the 64% your families gave.

screens.title: More likely than not
screens.prose: Drag the point along the curve. The caption gives the FWER for that many tests.
screens.question: Drag the point to the smallest $N$ where a false alarm is more likely than not.

hints.text: More likely than not means an FWER above 0.5.
The dashed line is 0.5. Find where the curve first rises above it.
$0.95^{13} = 0.513$ and $0.95^{14} = 0.488$. Which leaves the FWER above 0.5?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move the point until the caption first shows a value above 0.5.

byKey.thirteen: At 13 tests the FWER is 0.487, just below a half. One more test tips it.
byKey.twenty: 20 tests is well past a half, at 0.64. A smaller family already gets there.
byKey.ten: At 10 tests the FWER is 0.401. Ten tests at 5% do not make a half.

explain.text: At 13 tests the FWER is 0.487; at 14 it is 0.512. Solving $0.95^N = 0.5$ gives $N = \ln 0.5 / \ln 0.95 = 13.5$. So from 14 tests on, at least one false alarm is the likelier outcome.

screens.title: A family of one
screens.prose: Edge case. A researcher fixes one test in advance and runs it once, at $\alpha = 0.05$. Her family has a single member.
screens.question: What is the FWER for $N = 1$?

options.why: You treated one test as safe. A single test still passes noise 5% of the time.
That is the FWER for two tests, $1 - 0.95^2$.
That is the chance the test stays quiet, not the chance it raises a false alarm.

hints.text: The curve starts at $N = 1$.

feedback.correct: One test: the family's rate is the test's own 5%.

byKey.zero: You treated one test as safe. A single test still passes noise 5% of the time.

explain.text: With one test, $1 - 0.95^1 = 0.05$: the family's rate is the test's own rate. There is no multiplicity problem to correct. The problem appears only as tests are added.

screens.title: Only a 2% chance?
screens.prose: A researcher scans 20 indicators on data where none works. Indicator 7 has the smallest $p$-value, 0.02. Her note says: only a 2% chance this is luck. The curve is $1 - 0.98^N$.
screens.question: If all 20 indicators are noise, what is the chance the smallest $p$-value is 0.02 or less? Give 3 decimal places.

widget.label: Chance the smallest of 20 noise p-values is at most 0.02

hints.text: The smallest of 20 $p$-values is at most 0.02 exactly when at least one of them is.
One noise $p$-value is above 0.02 with chance 0.98.
All 20 above 0.02: $0.98^{20} = 0.668$. Take the complement.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance that all 20 $p$-values are above 0.02, then take the complement.

byKey.single: You used one test's chance, as her note did. She looked at 20 and kept the smallest, so the family's chance is what counts.
byKey.added: You added 20 chances of 0.02. Find the chance none is that small and subtract it from 1.
byKey.none: That is the chance no indicator gets down to 0.02. You want at least one.

explain.text: The smallest of 20 noise $p$-values is 0.02 or less with chance $1 - 0.98^{20} = 0.332$. That is one scan in three, not one in fifty. Her 2% is the chance for one test chosen in advance.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose: Each time you did the same steps. For $N$ independent tests of true nulls, each at level $\alpha$: $$\text{FWER} = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^N, \qquad E[\text{false alarms}] = N\alpha.$$
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: One true null stays quiet with chance $1 - \alpha$, since it passes with chance $\alpha$
All $N$ stay quiet with chance $(1 - \alpha)^N$, since independent chances multiply

hints.text: Start with a single test.
Independence is what lets you multiply the quiet chances.

feedback.correct: One quiet test, all quiet, the complement, then the numbers.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build from one test up to the family, then substitute.

byKey.comp: The complement needs the chance that all are quiet first.
byKey.all: Multiplying needs one test's quiet chance first.

explain.text: You built the FWER from one quiet test, then all $N$ quiet, then the complement. The expected count needs no independence: each test adds $\alpha$, so $E = N\alpha$. For 100 tests that was the 5 cells you tapped.

widget.solution:
import math
import random

def p_value(xs):
    """Two-sided z-test of mean 0, each x with sd 1."""
    n = len(xs)
    z = sum(xs) / n * math.sqrt(n)
    return 1 - math.erf(abs(z) / math.sqrt(2))

def count_significant(samples, alpha=0.05):
    """How many samples give a p-value below alpha."""
    return sum(1 for xs in samples if p_value(xs) < alpha)

rng = random.Random(15)
samples = [[rng.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(30)]
           for _ in range(20)]
print(count_significant(samples))
widget.prelude:
import random as _r
def _noise(seed, m=20, n=30):
    g = _r.Random(seed)
    return [[g.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(n)] for _ in range(m)]

`math.erf(abs(z) / math.sqrt(2))` is the chance of landing within $|z|$ of 0. The seed-15 run should print the 1 shown.
`return sum(1 for xs in samples if p_value(xs) < alpha)` counts the passes.

feedback.correct: Seed 15 gives one false alarm in 20 noise tests, the most common count.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the $p$-value against the examples first, then the count.

explain.text: `p_value` turns the mean into $z$ and the two tails into $p$. Seed 15 gives one pass, seed 4 gives three and seed 5 none. Over many seeds, 64% of families give at least one.

screens.title: The garden of forking paths
screens.prose: No formal family is needed. A researcher makes four yes-or-no choices after looking at the data: daily or weekly, trim outliers or not, start in 2010 or 2015, raw or log prices. She reports one test. This is the **garden of forking paths**.

state.caption: Each cell is one analysis she could have run.

screens.question: How many different analyses could she have reported?

widget.label: Number of possible analyses
widget.accept: 16 exactly: four two-way choices give $2^4 = 16$ paths.

hints.text: Each choice splits every path into two.
The grid has one cell per path. The first row alone holds four.
$2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each two-way choice doubles the number of paths.

byKey.choices: You counted the choices, not the paths. Each choice doubles the paths.
byKey.eight: You doubled three times. There are four two-way choices, so double four times.

explain.text: Four two-way choices give $2^4 = 16$ analyses, one per cell. Picking the one that works is like running 16 tests: if they were independent, the FWER would be $1 - 0.95^{16} = 0.56$. They overlap, so the true rate is lower, but far above 5%.

screens.title: The brochure
screens.prose: A signal vendor backtests 50 random signals, none with any edge. Each backtest is a test at 5%. The brochure shows only the best one, with $p = 0.03$.
screens.question: What is the chance that at least one of the 50 noise backtests passes at 5%? Give 3 decimal places.

widget.label: Chance at least one of 50 passes

hints.text: This is the FWER with $N = 50$.
The vertical line marks 50 backtests on the curve.

byKey.single: That is one backtest's chance. The vendor had 50 tries.
byKey.count: That is the expected number of passes, $50 \times 0.05$. The question asks for a chance.
byKey.none: That is the chance that no backtest passes.
byKey.brochure: That is the brochure's $p$-value for the one it kept, not the chance of finding one.

explain.text: The vendor finds a pass in 92% of such searches, and expects $50 \times 0.05 = 2.5$ of them. So a brochure showing one pass says almost nothing. Ask how many signals were tried before you read any $p$-value.

ideas: Each test of a true null passes with chance $\alpha$. Run $N$ and expect $N\alpha$ false discoveries.
The chance of at least one, the family-wise error rate, is $1 - (1 - \alpha)^N$: 0.64 for 20 tests at 5%.
Choices made after seeing the data are hidden tests. One test fixed in advance has no multiplicity problem.

formula.name: Family-wise error rate
formula.note: For $N$ independent tests of true nulls, each at level $\alpha$.

summary.trap: One pass among many tests is not a discovery. Each test's 5% is not the family's: 20 tests give 64%.
